prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Fifteen years later the old tollbooth keeper is still at his post but cannot break a twenty, regrettably, his brains blown out, or provide the forgotten directions. I did phone, what do you think? Before I can blink I am parked out front of the unbelievably small, unlighted house.I’ve got my finger on the buried bell, nothing. For hours I’ve been walking around, and I hate to be the one to tell you this, but no one is home in Zanesville, Ohio. My dusty toothbrush waits for me, of this I feel quite sure, my teenage image in the dust-dimmed mirror waits. Only now I’m afraid I’ll be forced to disturb the slow fine snow of dust that’s been coming down, year after year, on my blanket and hair, and put on my dust-covered clothes, and walk without making a sound, trailing my eternal lunar footprints, down the windless hall, and down the stairs at last. It’s not going to happen overnight. But one of these days I’ll arrive; I will go down to sit with the father. The elderly father, strictly speaking, of never really having been there.I will sit down and eat my bowl of dust like all the rest.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Fifteen, Before, For

outputs.L1:
Fifteen years later, the old tollbooth keeper is still at his post, but he cannot break a twenty—regrettably, his brains blown out—or provide the forgotten directions. I did phone; what do you think? Before I can blink, I am parked out front of the unbelievably small, unlighted house. I’ve got my finger on the buried bell: nothing. For hours I’ve been walking around, and I hate to be the one to tell you this, but no one is home in Zanesville, Ohio.

My dusty toothbrush waits for me; of this I feel quite sure. My teenage image in the dust-dimmed mirror waits. Only now I’m afraid I’ll be forced to disturb the slow, fine snow of dust that has been coming down, year after year, on my blanket and hair, and to put on my dust-covered clothes, and walk without making a sound, trailing my eternal lunar footprints down the windless hall and, at last, down the stairs.

It’s not going to happen overnight. But one of these days I’ll arrive; I will go down to sit with the father—the elderly father, strictly speaking, of never really having been there. I will sit down and eat my bowl of dust like all the rest.
outputs.L2:
Fifteen years on, the elderly tollbooth attendant remains in place, though he still can’t make change for a twenty—unfortunately, with his brains blown out—nor can he give the directions everyone has forgotten. I called, didn’t I? What did you expect? In the space of a moment, I find myself stopped in front of a house that is impossibly tiny and dark.

My finger presses the hidden doorbell. Nothing. I have been wandering for hours, and I’m sorry to have to say it, but there is nobody home in Zanesville, Ohio. I am certain my dust-coated toothbrush is waiting for me; so is the adolescent version of myself in the mirror dulled by dust. But now I fear I will have no choice but to disrupt the slow, delicate snowfall of dust that has settled, year after year, over my blanket and my hair. I will have to pull on my dust-laden clothes and move silently, leaving behind my endless moonlike footprints, along the airless hallway and finally down the stairs.

It won’t happen all at once. Still, someday I will get there. I will go downstairs and sit with the father—the old father, more precisely, of never truly having been present at all. I will take my place and eat my bowl of dust, just like everyone else.
outputs.L3:
After fifteen years away, the narrator returns expecting, or perhaps merely hoping, that something from the past might still offer guidance. At the old tollbooth, the keeper is still there, just as he had been long ago. His presence suggests continuity, a fragile link between past and present. Yet whatever comfort this recognition provides quickly fades. The keeper, though still in his place, is unable to help. He cannot direct the narrator in any meaningful way, cannot explain what has changed, and cannot restore what has been lost.

The journey leads the narrator to a small, dark house in Zanesville, Ohio. The house stands quietly, without welcome or movement. When the narrator arrives, it becomes clear that no one is home. The absence is not merely practical, but emotional and symbolic. The house feels abandoned, emptied of the life it once contained. Its darkness suggests neglect, distance, and the passage of time.

Inside the narrator’s imagination, however, the old room remains preserved. It is as though nothing has been touched for fifteen years. The toothbrush still waits where it was left, the mirror remains in place, and the blanket lies undisturbed. Old clothes hang or rest where they once belonged. Everything is covered in dust, but still recognizable. These objects become evidence of a former self, fragments of a life suspended in time.

Yet the narrator hesitates. To enter fully would be to disturb the dust that has gathered over the years. The dust represents more than neglect; it is the visible form of silence, memory, and abandonment. Moving through the room would break the stillness and disrupt the strange preservation of the past. The narrator fears not only making a physical mess, but also awakening emotions that have remained untouched for years.

Eventually, the narrator imagines going downstairs. There, they expect to sit with the father, whether he is literally absent or present only as a symbolic figure. This anticipated meeting is not one of reunion or resolution. Instead, it suggests surrender. The narrator seems to accept that they, too, may become part of the same stillness, the same dust-covered existence. In returning to the house, the narrator confronts the pull of inheritance, memory, and loss, recognizing the possibility of sharing the father’s fate in a place where time has stopped.
outputs.L4:
The speaker imagines returning to a childhood home in Zanesville, Ohio, but the return is not simple, physical, or complete. The house belongs to the past, and the past has become unreachable. Instead of a clear place that can be entered and reclaimed, the home appears through strange, dreamlike images: dust, emptiness, distance, and silence. Everything seems covered over, as though time itself has settled on the rooms and made them uninhabitable. The journey back becomes less a literal trip than an attempt to move through memory, where familiar places are distorted and where what once felt intimate now feels foreign.

This imagined homecoming is marked by failure. The speaker wants to recover something—perhaps a sense of origin, belonging, or lost childhood—but the effort cannot succeed. The home is no longer available in the way it once was. Even if the speaker can picture its rooms or approach its location, the emotional reality of the place has vanished. The people, sensations, and meanings that made it “home” are absent. What remains is only a haunted outline, a structure of memory filled with dust and ghosts. The speaker’s return therefore becomes an encounter with absence rather than restoration.

The surreal imagery emphasizes how memory works: it preserves fragments but not wholeness. The speaker can revisit certain details, but they do not lead back to a stable past. Instead, they reveal the distance between the self who remembers and the child who once lived there. The childhood home becomes both familiar and estranged, a place the speaker knows deeply yet can no longer belong to. This tension gives the passage its emotional force. The speaker is drawn back by longing, but the return only confirms that the past has been changed by time, loss, and separation.

In the end, the homecoming becomes a kind of ghostly ritual. The speaker does not truly recover the home but learns to inhabit its absence. Returning means accepting that what has been lost cannot be restored, only remembered. The past can be approached through imagination, language, and mourning, but it cannot be made present again. The childhood home in Zanesville thus becomes more than a location; it becomes a symbol of the human desire to return to origins and the painful knowledge that such a return is impossible. The passage is ultimately a meditation on memory, estrangement, and the feeling of never fully belonging—not even to the places that first made us.
outputs.L5:
**Fifteen Minutes Before**

Fifteen minutes before the meeting, Clara sat quietly by the window, gathering her thoughts. She had prepared for this moment for weeks, reviewing every detail and imagining every possible question. The folder in her hands felt heavier than it should, not because of the papers inside, but because of what they represented: effort, hope, and a chance for something new.

Before this day, she had often doubted herself. She wondered if she was ready, if her ideas were strong enough, and if people would listen. But now, as the clock moved forward, she realized that preparation had given her more than knowledge. It had given her confidence.

For the first time in a long while, Clara smiled. Fifteen minutes was not much time, but it was enough to breathe, to believe, and to remember why she had started. Whatever happened next, she knew she had done her best.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, literary prose poem about returning after fifteen years to a childhood home in Zanesville, Ohio, where everyone is gone and dust has accumulated like snow.
counterfactuals.output:
After fifteen years I returned to the house in Zanesville, Ohio, and found winter had entered without weather.

Dust lay over everything in pale drifts: on the banister, on the piano with its yellow teeth, on the framed school photographs where our faces had gone faint as moons seen through milk. It had gathered in the corners like something with intention. It softened the chairs, buried the lamps, made a white county of the dining room table. I stood in the doorway and did not cross it at first, afraid of leaving tracks.

Everyone was gone.

Not dead, exactly—not in that simple way—but removed, lifted, erased by the long hand of elsewhere. My mother’s blue cup still waited near the sink, holding a dry ring of tea the color of old pennies. My father’s work boots stood beneath the coat hooks, tongues open, as if they had been speaking for years and had finally fallen silent. Upstairs, the beds were made with the severity of graves. The wallpaper breathed in the hallway, a faint floral lung.

Outside, Zanesville continued its slow turning: the river dividing itself and joining itself, bridges shouldering the gray light, the hills crouched beyond town like animals that remembered glaciers. But inside the house time had not passed; it had accumulated. It lay on the windowsills, thick and white. It clung to the lace curtains. It sifted from the ceiling when I spoke my own name.

I walked from room to room, and each room became larger than it had been when I was a child. The kitchen was a gymnasium of hunger. The pantry was a chapel for extinct cans. In the closet beneath the stairs, where I once hid with a flashlight and a comic book, I found a nest of dust so deep it seemed to contain weather of its own—tiny blizzards stirred by my breath. I thought I heard someone laughing there, but it was only the house remembering how laughter worked.

On the refrigerator, a magnet shaped like Ohio held up nothing.

I pressed my palm to the wall of my old bedroom. Beneath the paint, the house trembled. I knew then it had been waiting—not for me, but for any witness who could confirm its dream. The ceiling fan hung motionless, a dark flower. My toys had become relics of a vanished religion: a red truck, one wheel missing; a stuffed bear flattened by years of invisible snow; a box of crayons gone waxy and mute, still arranged in the colors of commandments.

I opened the closet and a small avalanche fell.

For a moment I was ten years old again, standing under a storm that made no sound. The dust covered my shoes, my sleeves, my hair. It kissed my eyelashes with the tenderness of ashes. I closed my eyes and saw the old house full: breakfast burning, bathwater running, my sister singing wrong words to a song on the radio, my mother calling from downstairs, my father coming in from the garage with cold hands and the smell of oil. The rooms filled and emptied, filled and emptied, like lungs refusing to accept a final breath.

When I opened my eyes, no one had returned.

Only the house remained, vast and patient, snowed under from within. I understood then that childhood is not a country we leave, but a house that leaves us, room by room, carrying away the people, the voices, the heat in the walls, until at last we come back with our adult keys and find the door unlocked, the air white, and everything waiting beneath its quiet covering to ask what took us so long.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person flash fiction piece in a darkly comic, dreamlike style about an old tollbooth keeper, a failed homecoming, and the narrator confronting an absent father.
counterfactuals.output:
By the time I reached the tollbooth, the road behind me had folded itself into a pocket and the road ahead was chewing fog.

The keeper leaned out of his little glass hut like a turtle considering suicide. He wore a cap with a dead moth pinned to the brim and had the kind of mustache that suggested he had been waiting since the reign of a disappointing king.

“Homecoming?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Failed or successful?”

“I haven’t tried yet.”

He sighed and stamped my windshield with a rubber stamp anyway. FAILED, it said, in red letters that immediately began to crawl.

“That’ll be three teeth or a childhood memory.”

“I’m short on both.”

He looked me over. “You have your father’s eyes.”

“I’d like to return them.”

That made him laugh so hard his dentures fell into the coin basket and began singing “Auld Lang Syne.”

I had not been home in twenty years, unless you count dreams, letters returned unopened, and one drunk phone call to a cemetery where my mother was not yet buried. The town was supposed to be seven miles past the tollbooth, but in the fog it arrived all at once: church steeple, gas station, my old elementary school, and the house where I learned that absence could sit at the dinner table and ask for salt.

Banners hung from the telephone wires.

WELCOME HOME, whoever you are.

The marching band was there, though most of them were goats. My classmates lined the sidewalk holding casserole dishes and shovels. Nobody had aged correctly. Cindy Barlow, who’d once kissed me behind the gym and then told everyone I smelled like pennies, waved with the hand of an infant and the face of a taxidermied fox.

“You missed the parade,” she said.

“I thought I was the parade.”

“You were. That’s why it was so disappointing.”

At my old house, the porch sagged like a guilty man. The doorbell had been replaced by a tongue. I pressed it.

Inside, the living room was exactly as I remembered, except the sofa was breathing and the family portraits had turned their backs. My father sat in his recliner, or rather his absence did: a dent in the air wearing slippers, smoking a cigarette that burned from both ends.

I had rehearsed for this. In motels. In traffic. Into bathroom mirrors and the stunned faces of vending machines.

“Why did you leave?” I demanded.

The empty chair creaked.

“Don’t you dare give me silence,” I said. “That was always your best suit.”

A cough came from nowhere. Ash fell into the shape of a man, then lost interest.

“I waited for you,” I said. “At windows. At birthdays. At the hospital when Mom said not to call because you wouldn’t come, so of course I called.”

The cigarette hovered. The ashtray overflowed with little gray father-shapes, each one shrugging.

Then the tollbooth keeper stepped out from behind the curtains, carrying a ledger and a sandwich.

“Sorry,” he said. “He’s paid up through next century.”

“What?”

“Absence is a subscription service.” He licked mustard from his thumb. “Very popular with fathers.”

I turned back to the recliner. “I came all this way.”

The dent in the air deepened, as if settling in for a nap.

Outside, the town began applauding, politely at first, then with the frantic rhythm of rain on a coffin lid. My homecoming banner burst into flames. The goats struck up a waltz.

I picked up the cigarette and put it out on the arm of the chair. The room gasped.

“There,” I told him. “Now you’re gone from somewhere.”

The absence shivered.

For a moment, I saw him—not as a monster, not as a wound with a wallet, but as a small frightened man running out of doors until the world kindly stopped offering them. Then he vanished again, which was his only real talent.

When I left, the tollbooth keeper was waiting at the end of the driveway with his basket.

“Exit fee,” he said.

“I paid coming in.”

“That was for hope.”

“What’s this for?”

“Experience.”

I opened my mouth to protest, and a baby tooth fell into my palm, though I was forty-six and had long ago sold my innocence for rent.

The keeper accepted it, held it up to the fog, and nodded.

“Good,” he said. “Still some root on it.”

I drove away from home, or what had been dressed up as home for the occasion. In the rearview mirror, the house grew smaller, then younger, then impossible. The road unfolded ahead of me one white line at a time.

At the tollbooth, the old man raised the gate.

“Will I have to come back?” I asked.

He smiled, showing every tooth he had ever collected.

“Not if you keep going,” he said. “But people do enjoy a rerun.”

Then the gate lifted, and I drove through, laughing so hard I nearly mistook it for crying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, haunting paragraph of experimental fiction involving a road trip, a dead tollbooth attendant, an unlit house, a buried doorbell, and a bedroom preserved under dust.
counterfactuals.output: By the time we reached the last toll plaza, the highway had narrowed into a strip of black ribbon pulled tight between marshes, and the attendant was already dead in his booth, chin resting on the sill as if listening for exact change from beneath the earth; we drove on without paying, the barrier arm lifting by itself, slow and polite, and every mile after that felt borrowed. At the end of the road stood the house my mother swore had burned down before I was born, unlit in every window, its porch sagging like a tongue. In the yard, where no path led, my brother knelt and scraped away wet leaves until he found the doorbell buried in the soil, a small brass button cold as a tooth. When he pressed it, no sound came from the house, only from inside the car, from inside our mouths, from the dead tollbooth many miles behind us, ringing and ringing. The front door opened to dust so thick it seemed architectural, holding up the hallway, preserving our footprints before we made them. Upstairs, the bedroom waited: bedspread smooth, dolls facedown, a glass of water furred with gray, everything sealed beneath a patient snowfall of years. On the pillow lay a receipt from the toll road, stamped with tomorrow’s date, and under it a photograph of us asleep in that same room, mouths open as if still answering the bell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an uncanny monologue about trying to revisit a forgotten family house years later, only to discover that “no one is home,” ending with the narrator accepting a bowl of dust.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to know the house by its sounds.

The porch hinge spoke first, a thin complaint like a bird caught in a chimney. Then the floorboards, each with its own name: the low one by the umbrella stand, the sharp one under the photograph of my grandfather in his uniform, the long sigh at the top of the stairs. In the kitchen, the refrigerator hummed in its sleep. In the walls, the pipes knocked politely, as if asking to be let through.

When I came back, years later, I expected at least the hinge to recognize me.

The road had been widened. The fields on either side had been shaved down and parceled into clean rectangles of gravel and new brick, but the house remained at the end, smaller than memory and leaning away from the afternoon sun. Its windows were dark. Its roof had a soft sag to it, like a hat left out in the rain.

I carried no suitcase. I had not planned to stay. I had only wanted to stand in the doorway and be told, by wood and dust and the stale breath of old curtains, that something had kept my place.

I knocked.

The sound disappeared into the house.

After a while, I knocked again.

Behind the door, something moved. Not footsteps. Not quite. More like a room remembering the idea of footsteps.

I pressed my ear to the paint. It was cold. I could smell the old varnish, the mouse droppings, the sweetness of paper gone yellow. I said my mother’s name. I said my father’s. I said, “It’s me,” though I could not think why that should mean anything after so long.

From somewhere inside came a voice.

“No one is home.”

It was not a stranger’s voice. It was made of all our voices, poorly stirred together. My mother’s softness at the edges. My uncle’s gravel. My own child-voice hiding under the stairs. It spoke from behind the door, from above me, from the dead flowerbeds, from the mailbox packed with leaves.

“No one is home,” it said again.

I tried the handle. It turned.

Inside, the hallway had narrowed. Or I had become too large. The wallpaper, once blue with white flowers, had browned into the color of old tea. The mirror by the stairs had gone blind, silver peeling from its back in islands, so that when I looked into it I saw only pieces of myself: an eye, a cuff, the pale hook of my mouth.

“Hello?” I called.

The house answered by settling.

I walked from room to room. The parlor was empty except for the shape of furniture in the dust. The dining room table was gone, but its absence sat heavily in the center of the room, six chairs of shadow tucked around it. In the kitchen, the cabinets hung open. Their shelves were bare. On the counter lay a spoon furred with gray.

I remembered breakfasts there: burnt toast scraped over the sink, my sister kicking the table leg, my father folding the newspaper into smaller and smaller squares. I remembered my grandmother standing at the stove, turning to me with a bowl in her hands.

Eat, she would say. You’ll vanish.

But she had vanished first. Then the others, one by one, into hospitals, apartments, marriages, graves, countries whose names sounded invented. And I, obedient to the family talent, had vanished into my own life.

At the foot of the stairs, I found a row of shoes.

They were arranged from smallest to largest. My red rain boots, cracked and stiff. My sister’s school shoes. My mother’s brown heels. My father’s black church shoes, polished to a shine no dust had touched. At the end of the row was a pair I did not recognize, long and narrow, pointed toward the stairs as if someone had just stepped out of them and gone up barefoot.

I climbed.

The house breathed around me.

At the landing, the bedroom doors stood open. My parents’ room smelled of lavender and damp plaster. The bed was stripped to the mattress, which bore the faint hollow of two bodies sleeping back to back. In my old room, the ceiling still held the glow-in-the-dark stars I had pasted there, though they were pale now and visible even in daylight, a dead little sky.

On the pillow was a note written in dust.

I leaned close.

It said: We waited.

The words blurred when I exhaled.

I wanted then to leave. I wanted the road, the widened road, the gravel, the new houses with their clean windows and living people inside them. But at the end of the hall, where there had never been a door before, there was one now.

Light showed beneath it.

I knew, with the certainty one has in dreams and family stories, that I was expected.

So I opened it.

The room beyond was the kitchen again, but not the ruined one downstairs. This kitchen was warm. The curtains were whole. Evening pressed blue at the windows. The table was set for everyone: my parents, my sister, my grandmother, the uncles whose names had become arguments, the babies who had grown old without me. Their chairs were occupied by coats, by folded blankets, by heaps of hair, by framed photographs turned facedown.

At the stove stood someone with her back to me.

She was small and bent. She wore my grandmother’s apron.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I came as soon as I remembered.”

“No,” she said. “You came as soon as you forgot enough.”

She turned. Her face was not a face but a place where faces had been. I saw my mother’s cheek, my father’s brow, my own eyes when I was young and feverish. Then it was only dust held in the shape of kindness.

She ladled something from a pot into a bowl.

“I was told no one was home,” I said.

She smiled, and the smile ran through all the empty chairs.

“That’s right.”

She placed the bowl before me.

It was white china with a blue rim. The same bowl I had eaten from as a child. The one with the hairline crack like a river.

Inside was dust. Fine, gray, softly heaped. It gave off no steam. It smelled of attics, hymnals, skin, flour, long summers, closed bedrooms, and the underside of beds where children hide and listen to adults becoming ghosts.

“I’m not hungry,” I said.

“You are,” she told me. “You have always been.”

The chairs creaked. The coats leaned closer. Somewhere downstairs, the front door closed by itself, gently, like a mouth.

I understood then that houses do not keep us. They digest us slowly. They take our footsteps, our quarrels, the oil from our hands, the breath we leave in curtains, the names shouted up stairwells, the crumbs swept into corners. They grind all of it down to one thing and wait for us to come back and call it memory.

So I sat.

I folded my hands as I had been taught.

And when she offered it to me, I accepted a bowl of dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bleak absurdist prose passage in the style of contemporary American literary fiction, with themes of memory, absence, adolescence, and returning to a father who was never really there.
counterfactuals.output:
By the time I came back, the town had misplaced itself.

The gas station was now a vape shop called CLOUD COUNTY. The elementary school had been converted into storage units, each classroom sealed behind a corrugated metal door. Our old house sat at the end of Juniper Drive like a bad tooth no one could afford to pull. The porch sagged in the middle, as if it were tired of pretending to welcome anyone.

I had not seen my father in nine years, unless you counted the way I saw him in reflective surfaces: in the black window of the laundromat, in the turned-off television, in the dull spoon I used to eat cereal over the sink. He had written once, on the back of a receipt for motor oil. Come home if you want. No signature. No punctuation. The receipt was dated three months before he mailed it, which seemed like him. Even his invitations arrived late to themselves.

When I knocked, nobody answered. Then nobody continued answering. I stood there with my duffel bag and my adult face, feeling the old adolescent panic crawl out from wherever it had been hibernating. The panic wore my eighth-grade gym shorts. It smelled like cafeteria milk.

Inside, the house had been rearranged by neglect. Dust had found every surface and made a religion of it. A ceiling stain bloomed above the couch in the shape of a continent no one would ever discover. In the kitchen, the clock had stopped at 4:17, a time so specific it seemed accusatory.

My father was in the garage, sitting in a lawn chair between two broken lawnmowers. He was thinner than I remembered, which was impossible, because in memory he had always been mostly absence: a man-shaped weather event, a door closing, a truck starting in the dark. His hair had gone white in uneven patches, like something left out in the sun.

“You got tall,” he said.

“I’m thirty-one.”

He nodded, as though this explained not only my height but the general failure of the century.

We did not embrace. We had never been an embracing family. Our tenderness, when it appeared, tended to do so as an error in translation. He pointed to a second lawn chair with the grave courtesy of a priest offering communion, and I sat. Between us, a cardboard box held old extension cords, a deflated basketball, and a family of dead beetles arranged in what looked like a meeting.

For a while we listened to the house settle. Or maybe the house was laughing. It was hard to tell with houses, once they had outlived their purpose.

“I kept your room,” he said.

This was not true in any meaningful sense. My room had never been mine so much as a place where I stored my body during adolescence. I had lain there for years beneath a poster of a band I no longer liked, practicing disappearing. I had believed adulthood would be a clean exit. Instead it had been a larger room with worse lighting.

He coughed into his fist. “You hungry?”

“No.”

“Me neither.”

Then we sat with our not-hunger, which was familiar and almost intimate.

I wanted to ask him where he had been when I was thirteen and suspended for drawing a noose in the margin of my math homework. I wanted to ask why he missed my graduation but remembered to renew the truck registration. I wanted to ask if he had ever looked at me and seen a son, or if I had been only another object in the house, like the toaster that shocked you if you touched it wrong.

Instead I said, “The town looks different.”

He smiled a little. “It got ugly.”

“It was always ugly.”

“Yeah,” he said. “But now it knows.”

In the dying light, the garage filled with the gold of a world pretending to forgive itself. My father’s hands rested on his knees, spotted and nicked, hands that had fixed engines and patched drywall and failed, somehow, to touch my shoulder when I needed them to. I watched them carefully, as if they might reveal the trick. As if absence were a machine and he, at last, might show me where the missing part had gone.

But he only leaned back, closing his eyes against the sun.

For a moment I was fifteen again, waiting for him to say something that would change the past. For a moment he was my father, which is to say a chair occupied by silence. Somewhere in the neighborhood a dog barked with great conviction at nothing, and nothing, loyal as ever, barked back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
